definition: The family of electromagnetic waves in order of frequency: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays, with frequency increasing and wavelength decreasing along that list.
A transverse wave such as light, radio waves or X-rays; all electromagnetic waves travel at the same high speed in a vacuum. (Extended: that speed is $3.0 \times 10^8\ \text{m/s}$.)
The electromagnetic waves with the longest wavelength and lowest frequency, used for radio and TV broadcasts, radio astronomy and RFID tags.
Electromagnetic waves between radio waves and infrared, used for satellite communication, mobile phones and microwave ovens; too much exposure heats body cells internally.
Electromagnetic waves with a higher frequency than violet light, used for security marking and sterilising water; too much exposure damages skin and eye cells and can cause skin cancer.

Electromagnetic waves between ultraviolet and gamma rays that pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone, used in medical and security scanning; too much exposure damages cells or causes mutations.

The electromagnetic waves with the highest frequency and shortest wavelength, used to sterilise food and medical equipment and to detect and treat cancer; too much exposure damages cells or causes mutations.
A signal that varies continuously and can take any value within its range.
A signal with only two values, 1 and 0. It can carry data at a high rate, and because it can be regenerated accurately it can be sent over long distances.
